rationale: The literature on DHX9-related neurodevelopmental disorder (OMIM #620988) confirms that dysmorphic facial features lack pathognomonic distinctiveness on visual gestalt alone, with investigators noting no consistent facial gestalt or recognizable syndromic pattern across affected individuals. However, the quantitative assertion that dysmorphic features are present in a strict >60% majority is conflicted by primary cohort data: in the seminal characterizing cohort by Calame et al. (2023), dysmorphic facial features were documented in only 8 of 14 (57.1%) assessed individuals. Furthermore, additional reports (e.g., Yamada et al., 2023) highlight cardinal findings like short stature, intellectual disability, and cardiomyopathy without establishing recurrent craniofacial signs.

evidence.text: In a cohort of 20 individuals harboring pathogenic heterozygous DHX9 variants, dysmorphic facial features were reported in 8 of 14 clinically evaluated individuals (57.1%). The authors explicitly concluded that individuals lacked a consistent facial gestalt or a recognizable pattern of malformation, directly confirming the absence of distinct visual gestalt while failing to meet the hypothesized >60% threshold.

source.title: Monoallelic variation in DHX9, the gene encoding the DExH-box helicase DHX9, underlies neurodevelopment disorders and Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease
source.journal: The American Journal of Human Genetics
source.quote: Using exome sequencing and family-based rare-variant analyses, we identified 20 individuals with de novo, ultra-rare, heterozygous missense or loss-of-function (LoF) DHX9 variant alleles.

evidence.text: Characterization of a patient with a heterozygous de novo missense DHX9 variant (p.Gly414Arg) presented with short stature, intellectual disability, and left ventricular non-compaction cardiomyopathy, without prominent or distinct craniofacial dysmorphism being established as a defining hallmark.

source.title: Heterozygous loss-of-function DHX9 variants are associated with neurodevelopmental disorders: Human genetic and experimental evidences
source.quote: Herein, we report a patients with a heterozygous de novo missense variant, p.(Gly414Arg) of DHX9 who presented with a short stature, intellectual disability, and ventricular non-compaction cardiomyopathy.

evidence.text: Genomics England PanelApp curates DHX9 for intellectual disability, citing severe intellectual disability, autism, epilepsy, and dysmorphic facial features as phenotypic associations, but without attributing a specific pathognomonic facial gestalt.

source.title: Intellectual disability (Version 11.31)
source.quote: DHX9. 2 reviews. 2 green, MONOALLELIC, autosomal or pseudoautosomal ... Autism and epilepsy, severe intellectual disability and dysmorphic facial features.

conflicts: The hypothesis posits that dysmorphic facial features are present in the majority (>60%) of affected individuals, but the primary defining cohort (Calame et al., 2023) identified dysmorphic features in 8/14 assessed individuals (57.1%), falling below 60%.

new_directions.question_text: Does objective 3D facial imaging and machine-learning gestalt matching (e.g., GestaltMatcher/DeepGestalt) distinguish DHX9-related NDD from other RNA helicase-associated disorders (DDX3X, DHX30, DDX6)?
new_directions.rationale: While qualitative visual inspection fails to define a pathognomonic facies, automated deep facial phenotyping can detect subtle sub-visual mathematical signatures across cohorts.

new_directions.question_text: Do nuclear localization signal (NLS) missense variants correlate with higher penetrance of specific facial dysmorphisms compared to loss-of-function (LoF) variants?
new_directions.rationale: Calame et al. noted genotype-phenotype correlations where NLS variants cause severe NDD phenotypes and aberrant cytoplasmic retention whereas LoF variants cause milder traits.
